tagline: Pine forests and high meadows on the road to the North Rim
intro: The Kaibab Plateau–North Rim Parkway runs south from Jacob Lake through high forests and meadows to the Grand Canyon’s North Rim. The Forest Service describes a 44-mile drive past ponds and limestone outcrops, with ponderosa pine, fir and quaking aspen among its trees. It is a National Scenic Byway as well as a National Forest Scenic Byway and State Scenic Parkway. The Forest Service highlights the different plant communities along the road and their opportunities for viewing wildflowers.

A dirt road reached the North Rim by 1927, became a gravel road by 1935 and was paved by 1938. It received the SR 67 number in 1941. The Grand Canyon Lodge complex was built in 1927–1928, during the same period of North Rim development. Its main building burned in 1932, was rebuilt in 1936–1937 and was destroyed again in the Dragon Bravo Fire in July 2025.

From Jacob Lake’s junction with US 89A, the route winds through the woods toward Deer Lake and the narrow meadow north of the park entrance. Beyond the entrance, the road continues through North Rim to the lodge site and Bright Angel Point trail area. The park section is maintained by the National Park Service; Arizona maintains the road north of the entrance.

moments.title: Jacob Lake Lookout Tower
moments.text: An 80-foot steel tower with a seven-foot-square metal cab marks the Jacob Lake lookout. The Civilian Conservation Corps built it in 1934. The lookout description records an Osborne Fire Finder inside the cab. The tower appears on both the National Register of Historic Places and the National Historic Lookout Register.

moments.title: Kaibab meadows
moments.text: North of the park entrance, the road follows a narrow meadow edged with evergreen trees. The Forest Service’s description of this drive places sub-alpine meadows and grasslands alongside mixed conifer forest, ponds and limestone outcrops. Each supports a different plant community, with wildflowers including silverweed cinquefoil and purple-white owl’s-clover. The plateau’s cool forests are home to the Kaibab squirrel, which is confined to this region. Aspen, spruce-fir and ponderosa pine cover this high country, contrasting with the arid lowlands that surround the plateau.

moments.title: Bright Angel Point
moments.text: The Bright Angel Point trail follows a ridge at the end of the Bright Angel Peninsula to a view across the canyon. Its documented route begins on the south side of the Grand Canyon Lodge complex. That setting changed in July 2025 when the Dragon Bravo Fire destroyed the lodge’s main building. The building lost was a replacement: after the 1932 fire, the lodge was rebuilt using much of the original stonework, without its former second story and observation tower. The original lodge complex used native Kaibab Limestone and timber, materials chosen to harmonize with the rocky, forested setting.

practical: Kaibab meadows: The Forest Service says heavy winter snow normally closes SR 67 from November through mid-May. Services along the route are limited. (checked 2026-10-11)

sources.label: U.S. Forest Service, Kaibab Plateau Scenic Drive
